planting.note: Plant the corm in fall in gritty, sharply draining soil and keep it completely dry through its summer dormancy.

directions: This Mediterranean aroid from Corsica, Sardinia, and the Balearic Islands grows from a dormant corm that should be planted in fall for a late-spring display. The hooded, hairy-margined spathe opens around a shaggy spadix and is pollinated by flies drawn to its notoriously foul carrion scent, so give it a spot away from outdoor seating areas. Grow it in gritty, fast-draining soil in sheltered partial shade, and withhold all water once the leathery leaf dies back for summer rest. In colder zones, grow it in a container so it can be moved under cover for winter protection.

planting.note: Plant corms shallowly in fall in a gritty, fast-draining rock-garden or alpine-pot mix and keep bone dry over summer.

directions: This diminutive aroid from Crete and southern Turkey produces ground-hugging, cream-and-pink speckled spathes directly from the corm before its leaves emerge, and unlike many relatives it is pleasantly fragrant rather than foul-smelling. Plant the small corms shallowly in fall in a gritty, fast-draining mix, in a sheltered rock-garden pocket or alpine pot. It demands a baking-dry summer dormancy and resents winter wet, so give it full sun and sharp drainage, or grow it in a cold frame in rainy climates. Because the flowers sit almost flush with the soil, raising the bed or pot slightly helps show them off.

planting.note: Best grown in a container or alpine house in very gritty, mineral soil with a guaranteed dry summer dormancy.

directions: Purdy's fritillary is a stony-scree specialist from California's mountains, producing waxy white bells finely streaked with red and brown on stems 9 to 12 inches tall. Hardy across USDA zones 6 through 9, it is nonetheless particular about drainage and is usually grown in containers or an alpine house so its dry summer rest can be guaranteed. Plant bulbs in fall in a very gritty, mineral soil mix with little organic matter, in full sun, and keep bone dry from the time the leaves senesce until fall rains return. It makes a good entry point for gardeners wanting to try the trickier western fritillaries.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall into deep, well-drained soil and avoid any supplemental irrigation after bloom.

directions: This is a taller, larger-flowered form of mission bells restricted in the wild to a very limited area of California. Like other western fritillaries it is a lily relative that must have a thoroughly dry summer dormancy to persist, so plant bulbs in fall into deep, well-drained soil and avoid any supplemental watering after bloom finishes. A site with full sun to light shade and sharp drainage, such as a raised bed or large container, suits it well. Because the species occupies such a restricted native range, propagated stock like this helps take collecting pressure off wild populations.

common_name: Sierra Fawn Lily (Earliest-Blooming White Trout Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs a few inches deep in fall in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun to light shade; give room to naturalize.

directions: Native to the foothills of the Sierra Nevada, this fawn lily is usually the earliest Erythronium to bloom, often opening dainty, nodding white flowers with yellow centers as early as February. Its marbled foliage is as ornamental as the flowers, and it thrives in exposed, lean, fast-draining soil that bakes dry over summer. Plant bulbs a few inches deep in fall, in full sun to light shade, and, as with its Klamath relative, it will tolerate modest summer water provided drainage is excellent. Give it room to naturalize, since established colonies slowly spread by offsets.

planting.note: Pot bulbs in late summer or fall in free-draining compost; water through winter-spring growth, then dry off completely in summer.

directions: One of the most colorful and vigorous forms of Cape cowslip, this South African bulb carries spikes of tubular flowers whose outer petals are orange and green and whose inner petals are edged in deep maroon. Hardy only to about USDA zone 8 to 10, it is a winter-growing, summer-dormant bulb best grown in containers that can be kept frost-free, or brought under glass where winters turn cold. Pot bulbs in late summer or fall in free-draining compost, water through the winter-spring growing season, and let them dry off completely once the foliage yellows. It makes a rewarding greenhouse or sunroom container plant wherever it cannot be grown outdoors year-round.
